analysis.one_liner: Creates universal subsidized health coverage for young children and uninsured pregnant women, paid for by tobacco taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill would have covered every child under seven and hundreds of thousands of uninsured pregnant women, but it had zero cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have guaranteed comprehensive health coverage to every child under age seven and every uninsured pregnant woman, regardless of income, through state-run programs. Families would pay sliding-scale premiums capped by income, with federal subsidies for all families, and the program would be financed mainly by a tobacco tax increase, with some of that money also paying tobacco farmers to switch to other crops. It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under seven and uninsured pregnant women, who would be covered regardless of income or preexisting conditions. Families at every income level would get premium subsidies, with the smallest payments required from low-income households. Tobacco farmers and workers in tobacco-dependent areas would receive transition payments, crop-conversion help, and job training paid from a share of the new tobacco tax revenue. Hospitals and providers would gain newly insured patients.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Young children and uninsured pregnant women

how_it_helps.text: It would make every child under age seven and every uninsured pregnant woman eligible for comprehensive coverage regardless of income, with no waiting periods and no exclusions for preexisting conditions.

The required benefits package would exceed average Medicaid benefits and include preventive care, dental care, prescription drugs, mental health and substance abuse services, and special services for children with disabilities or chronic conditions.
Every family, at any income, would receive a premium subsidy, and annual family payments would be capped by income — as low as $10 per child for the poorest families — with no deductibles allowed.

The program would be financed by higher tobacco taxes, which would also discourage smoking, and employers would be barred from dropping dependent coverage for young children or pregnancy benefits after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Smokers, who would pay higher federal tobacco excise taxes — a burden that falls harder on lower-income smokers. Employers offering dependent coverage would face new restrictions and a fee if they dropped coverage for children under seven. The federal treasury would also absorb projected savings from Medicaid and other duplicated health programs to help fund coverage.

drawbacks.text: The funding would come mainly from higher tobacco excise taxes, which are paid by smokers — disproportionately lower-income adults — rather than by general progressive taxation.

Part of the financing depends on estimated federal savings from Medicaid and eliminating duplicated programs; if money runs short, the bill explicitly allows the Secretary of Health and Human Services to impose limitations on covered services for the program's solvency.

All families would be required to contribute premiums and copayments regardless of income, and states could impose surcharges for enrolling outside the open-enrollment period, so even the poorest families would owe at least a minimum annual payment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is universal coverage for young children and pregnant women — the populations where preventive care pays off most over a lifetime — financed by tobacco taxes that also serve a public health purpose by discouraging smoking. The benefits to covered families would be large and direct; the costs are real but narrower, falling on smokers through a regressive tax and on employers through coverage mandates. The honest design concern is financing: because the bill taps projected federal savings rather than firm revenue, benefits could be trimmed if those savings never materialized.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Simon introduced the bill on June 15, 1995 and delivered introductory remarks, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill's action history shows no further steps after the committee referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died in committee, never having reached the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco companies, smokers, and employers that would have faced the new taxes and coverage mandates were spared. Uninsured children and pregnant women — 11.1 million children lacked coverage in 1993, by the bill's own findings — gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco sellers and employers; uninsured families gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Paul Simon
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on June 15, 1995.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on June 15, 1995 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Sen. Nancy Kassebaum
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: As committee chair in the 104th Congress, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill, no senator from either party cosponsored it, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill's main funding source was a higher federal excise tax on tobacco products, which raises prices and reduces sales, plus a new criminal prohibition on smuggling products meant for export. The industry's interest in the bill's fate ran directly against the children's coverage it would have financed.

The bill would not have created a government health plan; it would have required states to enroll all eligible children and pregnant women in private 'certified plans' and pay them premiums negotiated by the state, making private insurers the permanent delivery channel for the new coverage.

A share of the new tobacco tax revenue would have gone into a trust fund paying farmers and workers directly, funding crop conversion, job training, and economic development in tobacco-dependent areas.

Employers would have been barred from dropping coverage for employees' young children or pregnancy benefits, and a fee would apply to employers who terminated dependent coverage for children under seven after enactment.
Newly insured children and pregnant women would mean more paying patients, particularly for prenatal and pediatric care that is now often uncompensated.
